content: 1. Myelosuppression, including conditions such as anemia, leukopenia, pancytopenia, and thrombocytopenia, has been reported in patients receiving linezolid. In cases where the outcome is known, hematologic parameters have shown improvement toward pretreatment levels after discontinuation of linezolid. Weekly monitoring of complete blood counts is recommended for patients on linezolid, especially those receiving treatment for more than two weeks, those with pre-existing myelosuppression, those on concomitant bone marrow-suppressing drugs, or those with chronic infections who have received prior or concurrent antibiotic therapy. Discontinuation of linezolid should be considered in patients who develop or experience worsening myelosuppression. 2. Peripheral and optic neuropathies have been reported in patients treated with linezolid (Zyvox), particularly in those treated for longer than the recommended maximum duration of 28 days. Cases of optic neuropathy progressing to vision loss have occurred in patients treated beyond this duration. Visual blurring has also been reported in some patients treated for less than 28 days. Peripheral and optic neuropathy has been observed in children as well. Patients experiencing symptoms of visual impairment, such as changes in visual acuity, color vision, blurred vision, or visual field defects, should undergo prompt ophthalmic evaluation. Visual function should be monitored in all patients taking linezolid for extended periods (≥3 months) and in any patient reporting new visual symptoms, regardless of treatment duration. If peripheral or optic neuropathy occurs, the risks and benefits of continuing linezolid therapy should be carefully weighed. 3. Serotonin syndrome, including fatal cases, has been reported with the co-administration of linezolid and serotonergic agents, such as selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs). Linezolid should not be administered to patients with carcinoid syndrome or those taking serotonergic medications (e.g., SSRIs, tricyclic antidepressants, serotonin 5-HT1 receptor agonists, meperidine, bupropion, or buspirone) unless clinically appropriate and with careful monitoring for signs of serotonin syndrome or neuroleptic malignant syndrome (NMS)-like reactions. In urgent cases where linezolid is necessary and alternatives are unavailable, the serotonergic agent should be promptly discontinued, and the patient should be monitored for two weeks (or five weeks if fluoxetine was taken) or until 24 hours after the last dose of linezolid, whichever comes first. Symptoms of serotonin syndrome or NMS-like reactions include hyperthermia, rigidity, myoclonus, autonomic instability, and mental status changes such as extreme agitation, delirium, or coma. Patients should also be monitored for discontinuation symptoms of the serotonergic agent. 4. An imbalance in mortality was observed in an open-label study of seriously ill patients with intravascular catheter-related infections treated with linezolid compared to vancomycin/dicloxacillin/oxacillin. This imbalance was primarily seen in linezolid-treated patients with Gram-negative pathogens, mixed Gram-negative and Gram-positive pathogens, or no pathogens identified at baseline, but not in those with Gram-positive infections only. Linezolid is not approved for the treatment of catheter-related bloodstream infections or catheter-site infections. It has no clinical activity against Gram-negative pathogens and should not be used for Gram-negative infections. If a Gram-negative pathogen is documented or suspected, appropriate Gram-negative therapy should be initiated immediately. 5. Clostridium difficile-associated diarrhea (CDAD) has been reported with nearly all antibacterial agents, including linezolid, and can range from mild diarrhea to fatal colitis. Antibacterial treatment alters the normal flora of the colon, leading to overgrowth of C. difficile, which produces toxins A and B that contribute to CDAD. Hypertoxin-producing strains of C. difficile can cause increased morbidity and mortality, as these infections may be refractory to antimicrobial therapy and require colectomy. CDAD should be considered in all patients presenting with diarrhea following antibiotic use, as it can occur up to two months after administration. If CDAD is suspected or confirmed, ongoing antibiotic use not directed against C. difficile may need to be discontinued. Appropriate fluid and electrolyte management, protein supplementation, antibiotic treatment of C. difficile, and surgical evaluation should be instituted as clinically indicated. 6. Lactic acidosis has been reported with linezolid use. Patients experiencing recurrent nausea, vomiting, unexplained acidosis, or low bicarbonate levels while on linezolid should receive immediate medical evaluation. 7. Seizures have been reported in patients treated with linezolid. Some of these cases involved patients with a history of seizures or risk factors for seizures. 8. Postmarketing cases of symptomatic hypoglycemia have been reported in diabetic patients receiving insulin or oral hypoglycemic agents while on linezolid, a reversible, nonselective monoamine oxidase (MAO) inhibitor. Some MAO inhibitors have been associated with hypoglycemic episodes in diabetic patients. While a causal relationship between linezolid and hypoglycemia has not been established, diabetic patients should be cautioned about potential hypoglycemic reactions when treated with linezolid. If hypoglycemia occurs, adjustments to the dose of insulin or oral hypoglycemic agents, or discontinuation of these agents or linezolid, may be required. 9. Prescribing linezolid in the absence of a proven or strongly suspected bacterial infection or a prophylactic indication is unlikely to benefit the patient and increases the risk of developing drug-resistant bacteria.
